summary: Notre Dame Bay light at Cape St. John, lit in 1884 near the island where the Queen of Swansea was wrecked in 1867; the cast-iron tower is inactive and the light shows from a skeletal tower.

structures.note: Heritage statement gives 11.6 m; Lighthouse Directory 11.5 m. Inactive since 2014 (Lighthouse Directory).
Active light on a 5 m skeletal tower (Lighthouse Directory); Coast Guard list gives 5.2 m height of structure, square skeleton tower.
Two-storey keepers' duplex about 34 m (112 ft) from the tower, linked by a covered walkway (Lighthouse Friends).

events.note: Brigantine Queen of Swansea lost on Gull Island (Cape John) 12 December 1867; all fifteen came off the ship; LF says three crew and a passenger went back and were lost at sea, the 1868 letter says four of the crew; eleven died on the island (bodies found April 1868)
Bodies found on the island by men from a vessel in April 1868 and taken to Tilt Cove for burial
Erected by the Newfoundland Board of Works
Light first shown; Captain Mark Rowsell appointed first lightkeeper (Lighthouse Friends)
Flat-roofed fog alarm building with attached keepers' dwelling added
Two new keepers' residences (a duplex and a single dwelling) built, 1960-61; two diesel generators
Classified a Recognized Federal Heritage Building
Historic cast-iron tower inactive since 2014; active light moved to a 5 m skeletal tower (date of the move not given)
Ownership being transferred in 2014; recipient not named (Lighthouse Directory)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The heritage statement gives the cast-iron tower as 11.6 m high. Lighthouse Directory gives 11.5 m (38 ft). Both describe the historic tower; the record's 5.2 m tower is the Coast Guard's figure for the skeletal tower that now carries the light. The record is kept, with both structures listed.

Sources differ on whether the light is still lit. The Coast Guard's list gives the light (Fl W 10s, 160 m) as seasonal. The Lighthouse Directory says the historic tower has been inactive since 2014 and the active light moved to a 5 m skeletal tower. The light is shown from the skeletal tower in season; the historic tower is inactive.

notes_for_editor: The 1868 letter is read from the Public Ledger reprint (Memphis, 1 June 1868), which copies a letter first printed in the St. John's Courier. Several other 1868 papers reprint it (Chicago Tribune, Richmond Dispatch, Alexandria Gazette, Nashville Union) and were seen only in search results; a second reprint would confirm the OCR'd wording. The headline is unreadable in the OCR. The letter's OCR is poor in places and the quotes avoid the damaged words. Lighthouse Friends names Captain Mark Rowsell's crew as the finders of the remains in April 1868. The letter describes the finders and the vessel that took the bodies to Tilt Cove, but does not name Rowsell; the story attributes the naming to Lighthouse Friends. The letter calls the doctor 'Mr. Dowsley'; Lighthouse Friends calls him 'Dr. Felix Dowsley'. Keepers: Lighthouse Friends is the only source read; it gives no dates for four of seven names and no roles. A genealogy page (WikiTree) gives Rowsell as keeper 1884 to 1904; it is unsourced and not used. Newfoundland government records (Board of Works reports, Journal of the House of Assembly) are not in the corpus and were not read; they are the likely source for the appointments, the 1884 build and the keepers' terms. The 1916 fog alarm and the 1960-61 buildings come from Lighthouse Friends only. The light's status: Rowlett says the historic tower has been inactive since 2014 and ownership was being transferred; the Coast Guard list still gives the light as seasonal. Confirm with the Coast Guard before publishing 'lit' or 'active'. The 1884 date is the built year in the heritage statement and the Directory; no first-light source separate from them was read. Chicago-area reprints and a Nashville reprint of the letter are not used. Gull Island (Cape Freels, Bonavista Bay) is a different light; the story says so once. Living-person rule: no keeper after about 1960 is named in this record. The ship's details (tonnage, Welsh brigantine, Find a Grave memorial) come from sites not used for facts. Check of this pass: the 1868 letter's OCR reads 'rour of the crew returned' (four); the story now says four, against LF's three crew and a passenger. The page image was not checked for that word, and the OCR is poor there; confirm before publishing. The Directory gives 11.5 m for the cast-iron tower and the heritage statement 11.6 m; the story uses 11.6 m (both give 38 ft). The letter's OCR credit line 'Chtttanooaa Frees and Times' sits before the 'Horrible Shipwreck' heading; the item itself credits the St. John's Courier, and the footnote follows the item.
